query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating an enhanced free energy sampling method (e.g., metadynamics or umbrella sampling) within molecular dynamics simulations will enable accurate and efficient computation of melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a broad range of high-entropy alloy compositions.
generation.material_initial_state: A disordered, single-phase high-entropy alloy in its crystalline (solid) state at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Implement an enhanced free energy sampling technique within molecular dynamics simulations to effectively overcome free energy barriers during the rapid solid-to-liquid transition.
generation.conditions: Simulations performed near the melting transition under equilibrium conditions across various HEA compositions; applied in a computational framework where temperature, pressure, and compositional variations are systematically varied.
generation.structural_mediator: Mapping of the free energy surface that captures barrier crossings and phase transition pathways, mediating the transition from solid to liquid.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced sampling methods alleviate the limitations of conventional MD by efficiently exploring rare events and barrier crossings, thereby enabling precise determination of the latent heat, entropy changes, and volume variations at melting.
generation.predicted_outcome: Simulations will yield melting temperatures, fusion enthalpies and entropies, and volume changes that align with experimental measurements within an error margin of approximately 5–10%, significantly outperforming standard MD approaches which typically exhibit larger deviations and longer computational times.
generation.baseline: Standard MD simulations without enhanced sampling, which have been shown to be less efficient and less accurate (error margins potentially around 20% or more) for capturing rapid phase transitions in HEAs.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to perform well for high-entropy alloys with disordered, single-phase structures; its applicability may be limited in systems exhibiting significant ordering, phase separation, or complex intermetallic formation.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative performance metrics, particularly the exact error margins and computational efficiency gains across the entire compositional space, remain uncertain until systematic benchmarking with experimental data is performed.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of molecular dynamics simulations incorporating the enhanced free energy sampling method on a representative set of HEA compositions. Parallel in-situ calorimetric measurements (or other high-accuracy experimental techniques) will be conducted to determine the melting point, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting. The simulation predictions will be quantitatively compared with experimental results.
measurements: Enthalpy of fusion using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC)
Entropy of fusion calculated from measured enthalpy and melting point
Volume change at melting determined by dilatometry or in situ X-ray diffraction measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and volume change differ from experimental values by more than approximately 10% across a majority of the tested HEA compositions, then the enhanced sampling method fails to provide the required accuracy and efficiency, falsifying the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy alloy nanoparticles bring hope to developing more efficient nanomaterials for high‐temperature applications. Nevertheless, the enhanced thermal stability of nearly equiatomic nanoalloys containing at least 5 metals is nothing more than theoretical speculation about the impact of thermodynamic contributions on their structural properties and remains to be proven. Here, in situ aberration‐corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and molecular dynamics simulations are combined to investigate at the atomic scale the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles (NPs) from 298 to 973 K. Both in situ STEM heating and atomistic simulations reveal strong structural and chemical evolutions in the NPs with the formation and melting of an AuCu layer at the surface of NPs at high temperature. This phase separation that appears progressively with temperature is driven by pronounced atomic diffusion that is surprisingly more active in these quinary nanoalloys than in monometallic and bimetallic subsystems. The structural stability of the prototype CoCrFeMnNi HEA has been extensively studied in a wide temperature range from 55 K to its melting temperature of ∼1,600 K at ambient pressure [19] [31] [37] [38] but to our knowledge, no polymorphic transition has been observed. Conversely, high-pressure studies remain a virgin area in HEAs. In this work, using in situ high-pressure XRD techniques, we observed the first polymorphic transition from fcc to hcp in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA, as shown in Fig. 1c . Therefore, some critical questions are how and why can an hcp HEA form at high-pressure and can it be maintained at ambient conditions? According to the d -spacing of the main reflections of both fcc and hcp (that is, (111) and (220) of fcc , and (100), (002), (101) and (110) of hcp , as a function of pressure shown in Fig. 2a ), it is clear that the hcp -(002) and hcp -(110) planes inherit the fcc -(111) and fcc -(220) planes, respectively. In addition, Fig. 2b shows no obvious volume collapse during the transition; both the fcc and hcp phases seem to have almost the same volume per atom and bulk modulus. This is similar to many other fcc to hcp martensitic transitions, such as in cobalt [39]

The LSF methodology proposed by Dong et al . [29] , [30] was adopted to describe the finite-temperature magnetic state of each alloy species in PM CoCrFeMnNi HEA. The root-mean-square magnetic moment m I ( w , T ) [30] , which is formulated as m I = ∫ μ 2 ⋅ x ( μ ) d μ with x ( μ ) being the spin-density distribution of longitudinal magnetic component μ , was used to represent the LSF energetics at thermal excitations in both the fcc and hcp phases. For the sake of computational feasibility of determining { m I }, we used the ‘fluctuating medium approximation’ and the ‘one shot from static equilibrium approach’ [29] . The present LSF methodology has been applied to PM bcc and fcc Fe and Fe-Cr-Ni alloy, and the predicted finite-temperature properties such as single-crystal elastic constants [29] , [30] , lattice expansion [34] and intrinsic energy barriers [39] confirm the accurate description of the magnetic state at elevated temperatures.

The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available. frame.system: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), which are multi-component metallic systems with a disordered solid solution state at room temperature, transitioning through melting into a liquid phase.
frame.goal: To accurately and efficiently determine the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the full compositional landscape of high-entropy alloys.
frame.limitation: Current approaches struggle with reproducibly capturing these thermophysical properties in HEAs due to their complex, multicomponent nature and the rapid transitions near melting, limiting both accuracy and efficiency.
constraints: Must be both accurate and efficient
Should be applicable across the entire compositional space of high-entropy alloys
Requires predictable quantitative performance and a clear range of applicability
Must include a decisive validation metric to rule out any incorrect approach
frame.regime: Operating near and at the melting transition, including the solid-to-liquid transition and subsequent liquid-phase behavior under thermodynamic equilibrium conditions.
prior_attempts: Traditional calorimetric measurements have been used to extract fusion enthalpy and related properties but often fall short in efficiency and accuracy for the broad compositional spectrum of HEAs.
Computational thermodynamic models and phase diagram extrapolations have been applied yet are limited by the intrinsic complexity and non-ideal mixing in HEAs.
